result.summary: Pausanias describes sites along the road from Thebes toward Chalcis: Teumessus, Glisas, Harma, Mycalessus and Aulis. He gives the local legends attached to each, including the Teumessian fox, the serpent's head, the miracle of Demeter's fruits, and Artemis's sacrifice at Aulis.

scenes.title: Teumessus and the tomb near Glisas
scenes.summary: Pausanias tells of Teumessus, its stone fox and the temple of Athene Telchinia, then the Argive tomb near the ruins of Glisas.

scenes.title: Serpent's head and Mount Highest
scenes.summary: Sites on the road to Glisas and Chalcis: the serpent's head killed by Tiresias, the mountain of Highest Zeus, the Thermodon, and Chalcodon's tomb.

scenes.title: Harma and Mycalessus
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the origins of the names Harma and Mycalessus and describes the miraculous temple of Demeter.

scenes.title: Aulis and Artemis
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the temple of Artemis at Aulis, the sacrifice of Iphigenia, the plane-tree, and the potters living there.
scenes.stakes: The Greek fleet is held back by unfavourable wind until Artemis is appeased.

alias_notes.explanation: Title linked to the Telchinians who supposedly founded her temple.
Hercules is said locally to be one of these ancient beings.

notable_quotes.reason: The miracle of Autumn fruits staying fresh a whole year before Demeter's statue.

analysis.text: The passage ties landmarks to myths, showing how place names and monuments preserved local memory.
Pausanias records competing local traditions, such as Tanagran and Theban claims about Harma, showing rivalry over mythic heritage.

legacy.text: The sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis became a major theme in Greek tragedy, notably Euripides' Iphigenia in Aulis.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that Aulis in his day had few inhabitants, all of them potters.

language_notes.text: Europa was a Phoenician princess whom Zeus, in the form of a bull, carried off to Crete; here a local tradition says he hid her at Teumessus.
The Telchinians were legendary early craftsmen and sorcerers, said to have lived on Cyprus and Rhodes; the title Telchinia is explained from them.
A stade was a Greek measure of about 600 feet (roughly 185 metres), so seven stades is under a mile and a half.
Ægialeus died in the Epigoni's expedition against Thebes, the second war, fought by sons of the Seven who had failed earlier.
Tiresias was the famous blind Theban seer; here he appears in an otherwise unrecorded act of killing a serpent.
Amphitryon, Heracles' mortal father, was a Theban hero; the battle against the Eubœans (people of Euboea) is referred to without further detail.
Harma means 'chariot' in Greek. Amphiaraus, one of the Seven against Thebes, was swallowed by the earth with his chariot; Thebans claimed another site.
Mycalessus is linked to the Greek verb for 'to low' (mykasthai), hence the cow's lowing. The cow guided Cadmus to the site of Thebes.
Refers to the Thracian massacre of Mycalessus in 413 BC, told earlier in his Attica book.
Idæan Dactyli were legendary Cretan 'fingers', mythical smiths and magicians; Pausanias here equates this Hercules with one of them, not the son of Alcmene.
Calchas was the Greek seer who declared Iphigenia must be sacrificed for winds; in the tradition mentioned, Artemis substituted a doe.
Brazen means made of bronze or brass.
'Not throughout good to eat' means the dates do not ripen fully; 'mellow' means softer and riper than those of Ionia.

context_notes.text: The Teumessian fox was a monster that could never be caught; Cephalus's hound Laelaps could catch anything, so Zeus turned both to stone to end the paradox.
Pausanias cross-refers to his earlier book on Attica and Megara, where he described the tomb at Pagæ.
Highest Zeus (Hypsistos) was a cult title of Zeus worshipped on mountain tops.
Artemis was goddess of hunting and wild things; torches and bow are her typical attributes.
Homer's Iliad (2.307) describes the plane-tree by a spring at Aulis, where a omen of a serpent and sparrows appeared.
Aulis was the harbour where the Greek fleet gathered before sailing to Troy.

literary_notes.text: The tale of the fox and dog turned to stone explains a local landmark by a legend, a typical way Pausanias links places to myth.
The brief, matter-of-fact explanation of the name shows Pausanias' guidebook voice, reporting local tradition without commenting on its truth.
Pausanias speaks as a travelling observer, introducing a wonder in a flat, matter-of-fact tone that lends it credibility.
The custom of accepting every kind of victim is explained by a story of the Greek fleet's becalmed wind, linking ritual to myth.
